Don't Go There
DOHNT goh THAIR
interjection, phrase (Gen X slang)
American slang of the early 1990s, picturing a conversation as a road and the unwelcome subject as a place one refuses to travel. Popular in African American and youth speech of the period and spread nationally by 1990s sitcoms and daytime talk shows, usually with a raised palm (the companion gesture of talk to the hand). Variants: don’t even go there, let’s not go there, I’m not going there.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Don’t go there draws a line across a conversation: that subject is off limits. Said with a raised palm, it can be a joke between friends, a warning before a fight, or a wall around a wound. The Christian observation is that Scripture itself says don’t go there — and means it — about some roads. "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men. Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away" (Pro 4:14-15). Some old offences should stay buried, too: "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends" (Pro 17:9), and "where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). A wise child learns not to go to gossip, to the old quarrel, or to the website his father has warned him about. But there is one place the phrase must never be used, and that is with God. The heart is full of rooms we would rather keep locked, and we say don’t go there to the Holy Spirit as often as we say it to our friends. The psalmist did the opposite: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts" (Psa 139:23). Christ already knows what is in the locked room, and He went to the cross for it. A father can teach both halves: refuse to go where sin lives, and never refuse God entrance to any part of you.

Webster 1828 Definition

Early-1990s American phrase (often with a raised palm) declaring a subject off limits; Scripture says it of the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14) and forbids saying it to God, who searches the heart (Psa 139:23).

expand to see more

DON’T GO THERE, interj. (Gen X slang, early 1990s, United States) Do not raise that subject; leave that alone. "You want to talk about my report card? Don’t go there."

Variants: don’t even go there, let’s not go there, I’m not going there; often with a raised palm, kin to talk to the hand.

The figure: a conversation as a road, and certain subjects as places one does not travel.

No entry in Webster 1828; the phrase is late-20th-century American slang.

Decode for parents: when your teenager says it, there may be a wound behind the wall — respect the moment, and keep the door open for later.

Key Scripture

Pro 4:14 — "Enter not into the path of the wicked, and go not in the way of evil men."

Pro 4:15 — "Avoid it, pass not by it, turn from it, and pass away."

Pro 17:9 — "He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends."

Pro 26:20 — "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth."

Psa 139:23 — "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts:"

Modern Corruption

Don’t go there can wisely close the road to gossip and old quarrels, or foolishly lock a room of the heart against the God who searches it.

expand to see more

A good fence. Not every use is a sin. Proverbs is full of places a wise man does not go: the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14-15), the repeated grievance that separates very friends (Pro 17:9), the talebearer’s fire that dies when no one feeds it (Pro 26:20). A teenager who says don’t go there to a dirty joke or a piece of gossip is doing exactly what Solomon told his son to do. Some roads are best never started.

A locked room. The danger is the same phrase turned inward. Men build walls around their pet sins and old hurts and post a sign: don’t go there. Friends learn to stay out; so, they hope, will God. But no room is hidden from Him, and the believer’s prayer is an open door: "Search me, O God, and know my heart" (Psa 139:23). What a man will not let Christ enter, he will not let Christ heal.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The conversation as a road → early-1990s American don’t go there (with raised palm) → don’t even go there; Scripture: go not in the way of evil men (Pro 4:14), but Search me, O God (Psa 139:23).

expand to see more

Old English gan → go — to move, to travel; there — that place

Figure: a conversation as a road with places one refuses to travel

Early 1990s American speech: don’t go there, don’t even go there

Companion gesture: the raised palm of talk to the hand

Biblical roads: avoid the path of the wicked (Pro 4:15); open the heart to God (Psa 139:23)

Usage

""Remember that haircut you had in seventh grade?" "Don’t go there.""

"Enter not into the path of the wicked (Pro 4:14) — the right place to say it."

"Search me, O God, and know my heart (Psa 139:23) — the place never to say it."
